questions.stem: In a persuasive text, the contention is:
options: the final call to action that appears in the text's conclusion
the main point of view the author wants the audience to accept
the strongest single piece of evidence that the author presents
the issue being debated, stated neutrally without taking a side
questions.explanation: The contention is the author's overall position on the issue. The issue itself is the topic under debate, which can be stated without taking any side.

questions.stem: An 'issue', in the study of argument, is:
options: a fact that every side of a public debate already agrees on
a subject of public interest on which there are several viewpoints
the single point of view that an author argues for in a text
a persuasive technique used to make an audience feel guilty
questions.explanation: The study design defines an issue as a subject or problem of public interest with multiple viewpoints. The single view an author argues for is the contention.

questions.stem: ‘Every summer our beaches drown in litter. A container deposit scheme in our shire would pay people to clean up after themselves – it's time the council acted.’ The contention is that:
options: the council itself has caused the shire's litter problem
the council should introduce a container deposit scheme
the shire's beaches become very crowded every summer
people who drop litter on beaches should be heavily fined
questions.explanation: The writer's overall position is that the council should act by introducing the scheme. The litter is the problem that supports the call; fines are never mentioned.

questions.stem: In a letter arguing that a town needs a new skate park, which sentence is a supporting argument rather than the contention?
options: Our town must build a new skate park, and it must do so this year.
The town council meets on the first Monday evening of every month.
Skate parks are recreational facilities designed for skateboarders.
Young people need safe, supervised places to spend their free time.
questions.explanation: A supporting argument is a reason for accepting the contention, here that young people need safe spaces. 'Our town must build a new skate park' is the contention itself.

questions.stem: ‘Phones distract students. Distracted students learn less. So phones should be banned from classrooms.’ Which best describes how this argument develops?
options: a chain of reasoning in which each claim builds toward the conclusion
a set of personal anecdotes that never arrive at a stated conclusion
a rebuttal of the opposing view followed by a concession to that view
a comparison of the results achieved by two different local schools
questions.explanation: Each sentence supplies a premise for the next, ending in the conclusion that phones should be banned. There are no personal stories and no opposing view.

questions.stem: An opinion piece opens with a story about a lost child, moves to statistics, rebuts a common objection, then ends by urging readers to act. Ending with the call to action mainly:
options: presents both sides of the debate equally, without a view
leaves readers with a clear sense of what they should do
supplies the main evidence on which the argument depends
introduces the issue to readers for the very first time
questions.explanation: Placing the call to action last means readers finish with the step the writer wants them to take. The evidence came earlier in the statistics.

questions.stem: An opinion piece about the safety of a river trail opens with a short story about a child who wandered off. Starting with this anecdote most likely aims to:
options: establish the writer's professional qualifications as a safety expert
set out the opposing argument that the writer will later rebut
engage readers emotionally before they meet the harder evidence
prove the trail is unsafe on the strength of this single case alone
questions.explanation: An opening anecdote hooks readers and makes the issue personal, so the evidence that follows lands with more force. One case cannot prove a general claim, and a careful writer would not rely on it to do so.

questions.stem: ‘A survey of 800 local students found that 61 per cent slept fewer than eight hours on school nights.’ This is an example of:
options: anecdotal evidence
expert opinion
a hypothetical example
statistical evidence
questions.explanation: A survey result expressed as a percentage is statistical evidence. Anecdotal evidence is a personal story, and expert opinion is the view of a qualified authority. Nothing here is imagined, so it is not a hypothetical example.

questions.stem: ‘When my neighbour's son was hit on that corner, the ambulance took twenty minutes to arrive.’ This sentence is best described as:
options: statistical evidence that proves a wider trend in the data
expert opinion from a qualified medical authority
a rhetorical question that invites readers to reflect
anecdotal evidence that makes the issue personal
questions.explanation: A story about one person's experience is an anecdote, which makes an issue concrete and emotional. A single case is not statistical and cannot prove a trend.

questions.stem: ‘Dr Anika Rao, a paediatric sleep specialist, warns that early starts disrupt teenagers' body clocks.’ A writer most likely includes this to:
options: provide a personal anecdote from the writer's own life
lend authority and credibility to the argument
appeal to readers' sense of humour about sleeping in
introduce a counter-argument that will be rebutted later
questions.explanation: Quoting a named specialist is expert opinion, used to make a claim seem trustworthy. The specialist supports the writer's case rather than opposing it.

questions.stem: A writer claims a new policy is a success because complaints fell by 40 per cent, but leaves out that the complaints line was closed for two of the months measured. This is best described as:
options: an expert opinion that strengthens the writer's claim
an anecdote that makes the issue personal to readers
a balanced presentation of both sides of the argument
selective use of evidence that misleads the reader
questions.explanation: Leaving out the closure hides the most likely reason complaints fell, so the figure misleads. Analysing argument includes noticing how evidence is chosen and framed, not only what it says.

questions.stem: ‘We all want our kids to grow up safe.’ The phrase 'we all' is an example of:
options: a rhetorical question, which invites readers to reflect
inclusive language, which builds a sense of shared values
an attack on opponents, which undermines their credibility
hyperbole, which exaggerates the danger for dramatic effect
questions.explanation: 'We all' draws writer and reader into one group with the same concern, which is inclusive language. Nobody is attacked, and the sentence is a statement, not a question.

questions.stem: ‘Callous developers want to rip the heart out of our town.’ This sentence mainly uses:
options: emotive language that casts the developers as heartless villains
neutral language that explains the details of the development plan
technical language that establishes the writer's planning expertise
inclusive language that invites the developers to join the community
questions.explanation: 'Callous' and 'rip the heart out' are chosen to provoke anger at the developers. Nothing about the plan itself is explained, so the language is far from neutral.

questions.stem: ‘How many more cyclists must die before we build proper bike lanes?’ This question is designed to:
options: introduce a neutral summary of both sides of the debate
suggest the answer is obvious and urge immediate action
gather data on cyclist deaths from the readers of the paper
show that the writer is still unsure of their own position
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question expects no reply; it implies that one more death is too many. It reveals a firm view rather than uncertainty.

questions.stem: ‘Without urgent repairs, the bridge could collapse during peak hour.’ This statement mainly appeals to:
options: national pride and patriotism
readers' sense of humour
family tradition and heritage
fear for people's safety
questions.explanation: The image of a collapse in peak hour is designed to make readers afraid for themselves and others. Nothing in the sentence touches on pride, humour or tradition.

questions.stem: ‘Each household will pay an extra $300 a year if the levy passes.’ This sentence appeals mainly to:
options: readers' trust in independent scientific expertise
readers' concern for the health of the environment
readers' financial self-interest, a hip-pocket appeal
readers' patriotism and their pride in Australia
questions.explanation: Pointing to a cost each household will bear is a hip-pocket appeal to self-interest. No expert or environmental claim is made.

questions.stem: ‘The mayor, who drives a gas-guzzling four-wheel drive, has no right to lecture us on emissions.’ This sentence is:
options: a concession that the mayor's argument has some merit
an appeal to the authority of an independent expert
an attack on the person rather than on their argument
a statistic that supports the mayor's position on emissions
questions.explanation: The sentence targets the mayor's own behaviour to discredit him instead of engaging with what he argues. It concedes nothing to his position.

questions.stem: ‘Teenagers today are glued to their phones.’ This sentence is best described as:
options: a call to action asking readers to respond to the issue
a sweeping generalisation that oversimplifies a group
a balanced claim supported by carefully gathered evidence
an anecdote about one particular teenager and her phone
questions.explanation: The sentence treats all teenagers as the same, which is a generalisation. No evidence is offered, so it is not a supported claim.

questions.stem: ‘Once again, the council has shown its remarkable talent for doing nothing.’ The tone of this sentence is:
options: admiring
neutral
sympathetic
sarcastic
questions.explanation: Praising a 'talent for doing nothing' says the opposite of what is meant in order to mock the council. The praise is mock admiration, not real admiration.

questions.stem: An editorial begins 'I understand the frustration of local traders' and ends 'It is time to stop whingeing and adapt.' The tone shifts from:
options: formal to nostalgic, as the writer remembers how the street once was
sympathetic to blunt, as the writer moves from conceding to insisting
angry to apologetic, as the writer gradually withdraws the contention
neutral to playful, as the writer begins to joke about the traders
questions.explanation: The opening acknowledges the traders' feelings, and the ending dismisses complaint as 'whingeing' and demands change. The writer hardens rather than apologises.

questions.stem: A columnist writes: 'Let's be fair dinkum: this tax is a dud.' The colloquial language mainly:
options: builds rapport with readers through a plain, down-to-earth voice
establishes the writer's academic expertise on matters of tax policy
presents neutral, verifiable evidence in support of the main claim
signals that the column is a formal, official government statement
questions.explanation: Australian slang such as 'fair dinkum' and 'dud' makes the writer sound like one of the readers. It works against an academic or official impression.

questions.stem: In a persuasive text, an accompanying photograph or cartoon is mainly used to:
options: replace the need for the text to state any written contention
provide neutral decoration that takes no side on the issue
list the sources of the statistics used in the written text
reinforce or extend the argument and position readers visually
questions.explanation: The study design stresses the role of visuals in supporting argument. Images are chosen to make readers see the issue in a particular way.

questions.stem: An article opposing a freeway includes a photo of a child on a swing in a park the freeway would replace. The image mainly:
options: shows readers how the freeway will benefit young families in the area
gives readers statistical evidence about the area's traffic congestion
presents the government's own view of the project in a balanced way
invites readers to see the project as a threat to families and community
questions.explanation: A child at play makes the lost park feel personal and precious, positioning readers against the freeway. The image supports the writer's opposition, not the government's case.

questions.stem: A cartoon shows a tiny politician hiding behind a giant stack of paper labelled 'REVIEW', while floodwater rises around voters. The cartoonist suggests that:
options: the government is using endless reviews to avoid taking action
the government is acting quickly and decisively on the floods
voters are to blame for choosing to build on flood plains
more paperwork is needed before flooding can be stopped
questions.explanation: The politician hides behind the 'REVIEW' while the water rises, implying delay dressed up as process. His tiny size also mocks his lack of stature, the opposite of decisive action.

questions.stem: A photo of a factory chimney is taken from a low angle, so the chimney towers over the frame. This framing most likely:
options: makes the chimney seem small, harmless and distant
places the viewer high above the scene, looking down
shows that the factory has been closed for many years
makes the chimney seem dominant and threatening
questions.explanation: Looking up at a subject makes it loom and seem powerful. A high angle looking down would make it seem small.

questions.stem: In spoken argument, 'stress' refers to:
options: the loudness of the speaker's voice overall
the extra emphasis placed on particular words
the speed at which the speech is delivered
the rise and fall of pitch across a sentence
questions.explanation: Stress is emphasis on chosen words to highlight what matters. Speed is pace, rise and fall of pitch is intonation, and loudness is volume.

questions.stem: A speaker says: 'Three students were injured on this crossing last year.' She pauses, then adds: 'Three.' The pause and repetition mainly:
options: signal that the speaker has lost her place in her written notes
speed up the speech so that the audience's attention is held
show the audience that the speaker is unsure of the statistic
give the figure time to sink in and heighten its emotional weight
questions.explanation: The silence and the single repeated word make listeners dwell on the injuries. A pause slows delivery rather than speeding it up.

questions.stem: A podcaster's voice rises sharply at the end of: 'And we're supposed to believe that?' Her intonation here signals:
options: agreement with the claim she has just quoted to listeners
a neutral summary of an expert's view on the issue
that she is reading a statistic aloud from a report
disbelief, inviting listeners to share her scepticism
questions.explanation: The rising, incredulous pitch shows she rejects the claim and wants listeners to doubt it too. Her tone is not neutral or agreeing.

questions.stem: A speaker slows her pace sharply as she describes her brother's injury. This most likely:
options: suggests the injury was minor and quickly forgotten about
hurries listeners past a detail that makes them uncomfortable
signals to the audience that she is about to tell a joke
draws listeners into the moment and signals its seriousness
questions.explanation: Slowing down gives weight to each detail and marks the moment as important. Hurrying past a detail would need a faster pace, not a slower one.

questions.stem: A speaker drops to a near-whisper for the line 'They never came home.' This change in volume mainly:
options: signals to the audience that the speech has ended
creates intimacy and gravity, so listeners lean in
suggests the speaker is ashamed of her own argument
makes the line harder to hear, so it matters less
questions.explanation: A sudden drop in volume makes listeners concentrate and conveys solemnity. It draws attention to the line rather than away from it.

questions.stem: A piece in a retirees' magazine argues for better bus services, stressing access to medical appointments and visits to grandchildren. The writer has tailored the arguments to:
options: tourists who are visiting the area for a short stay
the concerns and values of an older intended audience
secondary students who need to travel to school daily
bus drivers who are seeking higher wages and conditions
questions.explanation: Medical appointments and grandchildren speak directly to older readers' lives. The study design asks students to consider how authors use arguments to position an intended audience.

questions.stem: ‘Some say the new curfew punishes the many for the mistakes of the few. But ask the shopkeepers who sweep up broken glass every Sunday.’ How does the writer position readers?
options: by acknowledging an objection, then undermining it with an image of victims
by agreeing with the objection and calling for the curfew to be dropped
by presenting statistics that show the curfew has failed to cut crime
by attacking the shopkeepers for exaggerating the damage to their shops
questions.explanation: The writer names the opposing view and then answers it with sympathetic victims, a form of rebuttal. The shopkeepers are presented as people to pity, not people to blame.

questions.stem: The same argument for water restrictions is published once during a severe drought and once after record rainfall. It is likely to be received more favourably during the drought because:
options: record rainfall makes water restrictions a legal requirement
the context makes the issue feel urgent and personally relevant
readers in a drought are less likely to read any opinion pieces
the wording of the argument differs between the two publications
questions.explanation: The study design notes the impact of context on how arguments are presented and received. The argument is identical, so only the circumstances of the readers differ.

questions.stem: An argument for banning junk-food advertising is published on a parenting website. Which supporting argument is most likely to resonate with that audience?
options: The ban would reduce the advertising revenue that television networks rely on.
Junk-food companies employ many marketing staff in offices around the country.
Advertising codes have been reviewed several times by industry bodies.
The ads target children's pester power, making healthy choices harder for families.
questions.explanation: Parents are positioned by an argument about their own children and family life. Network revenue and industry staffing speak to quite different audiences.

questions.stem: An analysis of a persuasive text should focus mainly on:
options: how the author's argument and language aim to position the audience
whether the student personally agrees with the author's point of view
a summary of the issue's history, written in the student's own words
the student's own arguments for or against the author's position
questions.explanation: Analysis explains how a text tries to persuade, not whether it is right. The student's own view on the issue belongs in their point of view text, not their analysis.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the strongest analysis of persuasive language?
options: I agree with the writer that the plan is reckless and should be stopped now.
The writer thinks that the plan is reckless and says so twice in the article.
By labelling the plan 'reckless', the writer urges readers to see it as a danger.
The writer uses the word 'reckless', which is an example of emotive language.
questions.explanation: Strong analysis links a specific word to its intended effect on the audience. Naming the technique without explaining its effect is identification, not analysis.

questions.stem: Which phrase is most appropriate in an analysis of argument?
options: the writer is clearly right to say that
the writer forces every reader to believe
the writer invites readers to question
the writer proves beyond doubt that
questions.explanation: Analysis describes intended effects, such as inviting or encouraging readers, because audiences may respond differently. Claiming the writer 'proves' something judges the argument rather than analysing it.

questions.stem: The introduction to an analysis of a persuasive text should usually identify:
options: every persuasive technique used, in the order that each appears
the history of the publication and the size of its readership
the issue, author, form, contention, intended audience and tone
the student's own opinion on the issue and the reasons behind it
questions.explanation: An introduction sets up the analysis by naming the text's key features and context. Listing every technique belongs nowhere, because analysis should be selective and explain effects.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits a point of view speech to Year 11 classmates?
options: a dictionary definition of the key word in the speech's topic
a question or brief story that hooks listeners and leads into the contention
a complete list of every source the speaker consulted while researching
an apology to the audience for feeling nervous about speaking in public
questions.explanation: An engaging hook captures attention and moves into the speaker's position. Opening with an apology undermines the speaker's credibility from the first line.

questions.stem: In a spoken point of view text, phrases such as 'My second point is…' mainly:
options: appeal to listeners' emotions about the issue at hand
help listeners follow the structure of the argument
provide the evidence that supports the contention
rebut the claims made by the opposing side's speakers
questions.explanation: Signposting helps listeners, who cannot reread, keep track of where the speech is going. It organises the argument but supplies no evidence itself.

questions.stem: During a class debate, which question best probes an opponent's argument?
options: ‘Could you please read your whole speech to us again from the start?’
‘What evidence shows the ban would reduce litter rather than move it elsewhere?’
‘Why is it that you always seem to disagree with everyone in this class?’
‘Isn't it obvious to everyone here that your argument is simply wrong?’
questions.explanation: Good questioning tests the reasoning or evidence behind a claim. Questions about the opponent personally, or that simply assert they are wrong, do not engage with the argument.
